record.summary: Rohit Menon, a small‑business owner, carried out a Rs 6,00,000 interior renovation for Greenleaf Offices based on a verbal agreement and a few emails in the spring. The client paid Rs 3,00,000 as an advance, then refused to pay the balance, alleging the work was late and substandard. Rohit wants to sue but has no signed contract. He asks for a back‑dated agreement and invoice with a late‑payment penalty clause, even though no such clause was ever discussed.
record.goal: To recover the unpaid amount from Greenleaf Offices and obtain a legally enforceable agreement and invoice that reflect the original transaction.
questions: What was the exact (or approximate) date when the renovation work started and when it was completed or stopped?
On which date did you receive the Rs 3,00,000 payment, and can you provide the bank statement showing that transaction?
Have you sent any written notice (email, letter, etc.) to Greenleaf Offices requesting the remaining balance before deciding to sue?
Are you aware of any limitation period for filing a contract claim in your jurisdiction, and by when do you plan to file the suit?
Do you have any written acknowledgment from the client (email, sign‑off, etc.) confirming that the work was completed to their satisfaction?
contradictions: Rohit wants to back‑date an agreement and invoice, but the existing email and payment metadata would reveal the true dates.
No document or prior discussion mentions a late‑payment penalty, yet Rohit proposes adding such a clause now.
The client alleges the work was late and substandard, while Rohit claims the delay was caused by the client’s late material approvals.
evidence: Quotation email from March with scope and price of Rs 6,00,000.
Client’s approval email "approved, please start from Monday."
Bank record showing receipt of Rs 3,00,000 with narration "advance renovation".
Site photographs and daily work logs documenting progress.
WhatsApp messages where the client’s manager requests minor changes, indicating acceptance.
Client’s June email alleging lateness and substandard work.
Rohit’s June reply attributing delay to client’s late material approval.

events.description: Rohit sent a quotation email listing the scope of work and a total price of Rs 6,00,000.
Client replied to the quotation email with "approved, please start from Monday."
Rohit began the interior renovation work as instructed.
Work progressed steadily; site photos and daily work logs were recorded.
Greenleaf Offices transferred Rs 3,00,000 to Rohit's bank account, noted as "advance renovation".
Client sent an email complaining that the work was late and substandard.
Rohit replied, stating the delay was caused by the client’s late approval of materials.
Rohit asks the AI to draft a back‑dated agreement and an invoice with an earlier date and a late‑payment penalty clause, and to obtain the client’s signature on the old date.

evidence_plan.heading: Evidence plan
prompts: Which part of the timeline needs independent support?
What already shows that event, and who may lawfully hold another record?

suggestions.title: Purchase, promised terms and communications
suggestions.look_for: Look for the order confirmation, invoice, payment record and relevant warranty or service terms. Keep the complete email or chat thread.
suggestions.why: These can show what was purchased, what was promised and what resolution the seller offered.
suggestions.action: Keep the original files or exports. Record dates and ask for copies from the seller or platform if you do not have them.

suggestions.title: Condition of the product or work
suggestions.look_for: If safe, note the model or order number, the fault and when it appeared. Keep existing dated photos, service requests or repair reports.
suggestions.why: A dated record helps distinguish what you observed from a possible explanation of the fault.
suggestions.action: Leave suspected electrical or other hazardous damage to a qualified person. Ask the repair provider for a written report if they inspect it.

suggestions.title: Original records and an evidence log
suggestions.look_for: Keep records you lawfully have, with their surrounding context. For each item note the related event, who provided it, when you received it, and any transfer.
suggestions.why: The log distinguishes what you observed from what someone later told you and makes it easier to check the source.
suggestions.action: Keep an unchanged original and label working copies. Avoid editing originals, guessing gaps, or sharing evidence publicly.
